commentary.bottom_line: Nine sources, including two CHAI frameworks, NIST AI 600-1, and Utah HB 452, endorse requiring vendors to disclose data use, security, training-data lawfulness, and license terms during procurement, but no study has tested whether this review reduces harm. The recommendation rests on consensus and statute rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study tests procurement disclosure review, and no study documents how often the hazard occurs or what it costs. The nine endorsements include three frameworks, one guidance document, one statute, and four commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement of this kind does not support a certainty rating for effect, so the rating is no direct evidence.

Utah HB 452 (2025) lists compliance with federal health privacy regulations and user data collection and sharing practices for mental health chatbots, which may give the practice legal footing in that setting. NIST AI 600-1 and the CHAI playbooks treat training-data lawfulness as a diligence and contract matter. None of these sources reports whether disclosure changes vendor behavior.

The endorsing sources describe what to request, such as data retention settings, reuse of hospital data for product improvement, and patient data passing through vendor servers. They do not estimate the staff time, legal review, or expertise needed to evaluate these disclosures, so the cost of adoption at scale is unknown.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures whether structured vendor disclosure and review during procurement reduces data misuse, security incidents, or exposure to unlawfully obtained training data compared with standard contracting. Studies could compare organizations that use disclosure checklists with those that do not, tracking contract changes, rejected vendors, breaches, and review burden.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net organizations may have fewer legal and security staff to review vendor disclosures, and no data show whether the practice works under those resource limits.
